Container.Name: tldw-redis
Container.Overview: Redis for tl;dw (Too Long, Didn't Watch) - the job queue and cache the tl;dw API server runs its background work through. TWO CONTAINERS, STARTED IN ORDER: tldw-redis first, then tldw-server. There is no template equivalent of compose depends_on, so nothing enforces that for you. GIVE TL;DW ITS OWN: this container runs with a 512 MB memory ceiling and an allkeys-lru eviction policy, exactly as upstream's single-user compose file does, which means that under memory pressure it throws away the least recently used keys - acceptable for a cache and for this queue at upstream's sizing, destructive for anything else that might be sharing a Redis with it. STORAGE: the /data mount holds the append-only file, so the queue survives a restart. Losing it does not lose your ingested corpus - that lives on the tl;dw API container's own mount - it loses whatever work was queued. EXPOSURE: this template publishes no host port for Redis, so it is reachable only from a container on the same Docker network as this one, not from the wider network this host is on; there is still no password, so keep that network one you trust. See tldw-server.xml's own header for how that container reaches this one. IMAGE TAG: redis:7-alpine is a rolling tag, so unlike its sibling this container can take an upstream version change on an Update - see the comment at the top of the template file. The Redis command line is set in Post Arguments rather than as variables, because that is how this image is configured.
Container.Description: Redis for tl;dw - job queue and cache. Start this before tldw-server. Dedicated instance: it evicts under memory pressure.

Config.Name: Data
Config.Description: REQUIRED. Where the append-only file lives, which is what makes the queue survive a restart. Set an absolute path on a POOL (e.g. /mnt/<pool>/appdata/tldw-redis/data). Without it the queue is written into the container layer and lost on the next update - which loses queued and in-flight jobs, though not the ingested corpus itself. Unlike the API container's mount, this one does not care who owns the directory: the official Redis image sets the ownership itself before dropping privileges.
